344.title: Yitro: one person, one heart (Exodus 19:2)
344.hook: Rashi: at Sinai they camped like one person with one heart
344.howItsDone: Rashi's phrase 'like one person with one heart' is often quoted in Jewish teaching about unity, especially around Shavuot, the festival of receiving the Torah at Sinai.

segments.voice: Yesterday Yitro, a priest of Midian, showed Moses how to share the load. Your line was wisdom from outside. Today, still in Yitro, the people reach the mountain.

A family road trip. Six hours of who's touching whom, which song, why we didn't stop at the last exit. Then you arrive somewhere, the ocean maybe, or a canyon, and for one minute everyone in the car goes quiet and looks at the same thing. Nobody arranged it. The Israelites have spent weeks arguing in the wilderness, about water, about food, about Moses. Now, in the third month after leaving Egypt, they come to the mountain. And one verb in the verse doesn't match the others.
screen: `SIX HOURS OF ARGUING.` → `EVERYONE LOOKS AT THE SAME THING.` → `THEY COME TO THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: The verse says they set out from Rephidim, came to the wilderness of Sinai, and camped in the wilderness. Then it adds: and there Israel encamped before the mountain. In English, that sounds normal. In Hebrew, the first verbs are plural: they journeyed, they came, they camped. The last one switches to singular: vayichan, he camped. Israel camped as one. Rashi, the great eleventh-century commentator from France, following an older midrash, the Mekhilta, reads that switch on purpose. Everywhere else, he says, they camped with complaints and quarrels. Here they camped like one person, with one heart. Think who these people were: former slaves from different tribes, with different grudges, hungry, tired, frightened. Not one opinion, not one personality. But for this moment, one heart, turned toward the same mountain. Notice what Rashi doesn't say. He doesn't say they agreed about everything. One heart isn't one mind. It's a shared direction, a shared readiness. And the tradition ties this unity to what comes next: only a people camped like this, the commentators say, was ready to stand at Sinai and receive the Torah. A tiny grammar shift, from they to he, and centuries of readers have heard in it the hope that people who disagree can still face the same way.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you're often at odds with: a sibling, a coworker, a neighbor, someone across a political line. You won't agree on everything, so look for one thing you both want, their kids safe, the project working, the parent you share cared for. Hold that shared mountain in mind, and if you pray, hold that person there too.

345.title: Yitro: on eagles' wings (Exodus 19:4)
345.hook: "I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself"
345.howItsDone: Jewish teachers read Exodus 19:4 alongside Rashi's comment on the eagle shielding its young, and the image returns in the song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32:11.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Yitro, the people camped before the mountain like one person with one heart. Your line was one heart. Today, the first words God speaks at Sinai.

Ask someone how they got through the worst year of their life, and sometimes the answer isn't I was strong. It's: my sister moved in. My friends set up a meal schedule. My grandmother called every single night. Some people see only later that they were carried; at the time they were too busy surviving. Moses climbs the mountain. Before any commandment, before any thunder, God gives him a message for the people. And it begins by asking them to look back at how they got here.
screen: `HOW DID YOU GET THROUGH IT?` → `I WAS CARRIED.` → `BEFORE THE THUNDER, A MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the old Jewish translation: "Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself." Three things in one breath: what happened to Egypt, how you were carried, and where you were carried to. Not to a place, but to Me. Rashi, drawing on the Mekhilta, asks: why an eagle? Other birds, he says, carry their young in their claws, because they fear the bigger birds above them. The eagle flies higher than any of them, so the only danger comes from below, from a hunter's arrow. So the eagle carries its young on its wings. Let the arrow strike me, the eagle says, rather than my children. That's the picture the verse paints: a parent putting itself between the danger and the little one. The Torah uses the image again near its end, in the song of Moses in Deuteronomy, where an eagle stirs up her nest, hovers over her young, spreads her wings and carries them. One honest note: the Hebrew word, nesher, may mean a griffon vulture as much as an eagle; scholars debate it. Either way, it's a huge bird with a long reach. And the people the verse speaks to were carried before they knew it, through plagues and the sea and the desert, to the foot of this mountain.

segments.voice: Think of a hard stretch that's behind you now, and let the faces or names of those who carried you through it come, one by one: a person, a stranger, a teacher, a song, a community. Some of them you may never have thanked. If you pray, you can give thanks for them now; if not, stay with the names, and how much of the weight was shared.

346.title: Yitro: the first word (Exodus 20:2)
346.hook: the Ten Words begin not with a rule but with "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out"
346.tomorrow: Yitro: the last word is inside (Exodus 20:14)
346.howItsDone: The Ten Words are read in synagogue in the portion Yitro, in Va'etchanan in Deuteronomy, and on Shavuot, the festival of receiving the Torah; in some congregations people stand while they are chanted.

segments.voice: Yesterday God reminded the people they'd been carried on eagles' wings. Your line was on eagles' wings. Today, the mountain smokes, and the first word is spoken.

A new job usually starts with a handbook: hours, dress code, what gets you fired. A marriage doesn't start that way. Nobody opens a wedding with a list of house rules. It starts with names, and a story: who we are to each other, what we've already been through. The mountain is wrapped in smoke. Thunder, lightning, the sound of a horn growing louder. The people tremble at the foot of Sinai. Then the voice speaks the first of the Ten Words. It sounds like the moment for a rule. It isn't.
screen: `A JOB STARTS WITH A HANDBOOK.` → `A MARRIAGE STARTS WITH NAMES.` → `SMOKE, THUNDER, THE FIRST WORD.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." No command in it. No thou shalt. Just I, and you, and what happened between us. The very first Hebrew word is anochi, I. There's a shorter everyday word for I, ani; anochi is the fuller, weightier one, and the Talmud, playing with its letters, reads them as the initials of a short Aramaic phrase: I myself wrote it and gave it. In Jewish tradition this whole verse counts as the first of the Ten Words. That's the Torah's own name for them, aseret ha-devarim, the ten words or ten statements, not ten commandments. Traditions number the ten in different ways, and that's fine; this is how Jewish tradition counts. The medieval poet and philosopher Judah Halevi asked: why doesn't God introduce himself as the one who created heaven and earth? Wouldn't that be grander? His answer: the people at the mountain hadn't seen creation. They had seen Egypt. They had walked out. So God speaks through what they themselves lived: not the God of the philosophers, but the God of your own story. Everything after this, every rule about Shabbat and parents and honesty, rests on that first sentence. First a relationship. Then the rules.
screen: `I AM THE LORD THY GOD.` · `ANOCHI: THE WEIGHTY I.` · `TEN WORDS, NOT TEN RULES.` · `JUDAH HALEVI: NOT CREATION, EGYPT.` · then, large: `FIRST, A RELATIONSHIP.`

segments.voice: Remember one thing that once held you and doesn't anymore: a fear, a job, a habit, a diagnosis that turned out all right. Let yourself recall the day you knew you were out, and who or what brought you out. If you pray, you can say the verse's own opening, I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out, and hear it spoken to you; if not, stay with the memory of the open door.
Anochi. I. The first word God speaks at Sinai: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out. A relationship before a rule.
Your line: first, a relationship. It begins with I, and you, and a story. Until tomorrow.

347.title: Yitro: the last word is inside (Exodus 20:14)
347.hook: the final commandment, not to covet, governs the heart rather than the hands
347.tomorrow: Mishpatim: straight after Sinai, the details
347.howItsDone: Jewish law, following the Mekhilta and Maimonides, holds that the command not to covet is broken by acting on the desire, such as pressuring an owner to sell; Jewish ethical writers also treat envy itself as a trait to work on.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anochi, the first of the Ten Words: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out. Your line was first, a relationship. Today, the last day of Yitro, and the last of the ten.

Scroll through anyone's feed for five minutes: the kitchen renovation, the beach in Greece, the promotion, the couple who never seem to argue. Nobody stole anything. Nobody lied. And still a phone gets put down by someone feeling a little smaller, wanting what's theirs. Most of the Ten Words are about things you could see someone do or not do: make an idol, work on Shabbat, steal, lie in court. The tenth is different. Nobody can see you break it.
screen: `FIVE MINUTES OF SCROLLING.` → `A LITTLE SMALLER, WANTING MORE.` → `NOBODY CAN SEE IT.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation, the tenth begins: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house"; then the list: his wife, his servants, his ox, his donkey, anything that belongs to your neighbor. In Hebrew, lo tachmod. The first word was anochi, I, God's own self. The last word reaches into your own self. Abraham ibn Ezra, the medieval Spanish commentator, asked the honest question: how can anyone be commanded not to feel something? Wanting just happens. His answer is a parable. A villager sees a beautiful princess pass by. He doesn't lie awake longing to marry her, because he knows it's simply not his world. In the same way, says Ibn Ezra, a person who truly understands that what's yours is yours by God's gift will stop reaching for what isn't. The wanting quiets down because the frame has changed. The early rabbis and Maimonides read the verse more narrowly in law: you break it when you act on the wanting, pressuring someone until they hand over what's theirs. Deuteronomy adds a second verb, about desire itself. So there's a range of readings, from the hands to the heart. Either way, the list that starts at Sinai ends inside the chest. And with that, Yitro is done: an outsider's wisdom, one heart, eagles' wings, the first word, and the last.

segments.voice: Name, without scolding yourself, one thing in someone else's life you've quietly been wanting: their house, their job, their marriage, their calm. Then turn to what's actually in your hands right now, a person, a skill, a small comfort, this breath, and hold that instead. If you pray, you can give thanks for one of those things, and let the envy loosen a little.
Yitro. The portion we finish today, whose Ten Words begin with God's I and end inside the human heart.

348.title: Mishpatim: straight after Sinai, the details
348.hook: after the thunder come laws about workers, damages and loans
348.tomorrow: Mishpatim: the heart of a stranger (Exodus 23:9)
348.howItsDone: The civil laws of Mishpatim are studied through the Talmud's tractates on damages and property, Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia and Bava Batra.

segments.voice: Yesterday Yitro ended with lo tachmod, do not covet. Your line was the last word is inside. Today, a new portion, and a sudden change of tone.

A hospital lobby often has big words on the wall: compassion, dignity, care. The words don't wash anyone's hands. What carries them out is a laminated checklist by the sink, a chart at the foot of the bed, a nurse checking the name on a wristband twice. The big words live in the small print. The Torah works the same way. One portion is full of thunder, lightning, a mountain on fire and the voice of God. The very next opens, almost without a pause, with laws about servants, injuries, a goring ox and an open pit.
screen: `BIG WORDS ON THE LOBBY WALL.` → `A CHECKLIST BY THE SINK.` → `AFTER THE THUNDER, AN OPEN PIT.`

segments.voice: The portion's first verse, in the old Jewish translation: "Now these are the ordinances which thou shalt set before them." Ordinances, in Hebrew mishpatim: laws, judgments, the rules a court would use. And they're astonishingly practical. A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year. Dig a pit, leave it open, and an animal falls in: you pay. If your ox has gored before and you didn't keep it in, you're responsible. Lend money to a poor person, and don't charge interest. Take a neighbor's cloak as a pledge, and give it back before sunset, because it's what they sleep in. Rashi, the medieval commentator, stops on the first word. In Hebrew it's not just these, it's and these. That little and, he says, joins this portion to the one before: just as the Ten Words came from Sinai, so did these. For Rashi, the goring ox comes from the same place as the thunder. He also notices set before them, and says it means like a table that's set, ready to eat from, everything laid out clearly. That's the point of the portion. Sinai wasn't meant to stay on the mountain. It was meant to come down into the barn, the field, the loan, the paycheck. Holiness here doesn't float. It shows up in the fine print.

349.title: Mishpatim: the heart of a stranger (Exodus 23:9)
349.hook: "for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers"
349.howItsDone: Jewish communities often cite the command to love and protect the stranger when welcoming newcomers and immigrants, and the memory of being strangers in Egypt is retold every year at the Passover seder.

segments.voice: Yesterday Mishpatim brought Sinai down into pits, oxen and loans. Your line was holiness lives in details. Today, one law in the portion that keeps coming back.

Remember a first day: a new school, a new city, a new country. You don't know where the bathroom is, or which jokes are allowed. You stand at the edge of a group, holding your tray, trying not to look like you're looking for a seat. Almost everyone has felt that at least once. Most of us forget it as soon as we belong. The Torah, in the middle of laws about courts and bribes and fair judgment, asks the Israelites not to forget it.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY, HOLDING YOUR TRAY.` → `LOOKING FOR A SEAT.` → `DON'T FORGET IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish translation: "And a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Hebrew for stranger is ger, from a root meaning to sojourn, to live somewhere that isn't originally yours. Abraham calls himself a ger when he buys a grave for Sarah: a stranger and a sojourner among the locals. Later, in rabbinic Hebrew, ger also came to mean a convert to Judaism, someone who chose to join the people. But here, in Exodus, it means the outsider living among you: the immigrant, the foreigner, the one without family or land to protect them. And look at the reason given. Not because it's the law. Not because God says so, though God does. Because you know. The Hebrew says you know the nefesh of the stranger, the soul, the inner life. You've been the one at the edge, the one without rights. Use that memory. The Talmud counts how often this comes up: one sage says the Torah warns about the stranger in thirty-six places; others say forty-six. Either way, few commands are repeated so often. Even in this portion it's the second time; a chapter earlier, the same warning appears. It seems the Torah expected people to forget, and kept reminding them.

segments.voice: Bring back a time you were the new one: a school, a job, a country, a family you married into. Notice where you didn't know where to stand, and who, if anyone, made room for you. Then think of someone new in your life now, at work, on your street, in your community, and what would have helped you then.
Ger. The stranger, the one who sojourns among you. And the Torah's reason for kindness to them: you were strangers too.
Your line: you know the stranger's heart. Memory can be a kind of kindness. Until tomorrow.

350.title: Mishpatim: your enemy's donkey (Exodus 23:4–5)
350.hook: return your enemy's straying ox and help his fallen donkey up
350.tomorrow: Mishpatim: the widow and the orphan (Exodus 22:21–23)
350.howItsDone: Jewish law counts returning lost property, hashavat aveidah, and helping unload a fallen animal as commandments, and the Talmud's rule to help an enemy first is taught as training the heart through action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ger, the stranger, and the reason the Torah gives: you know the stranger's heart. Today, still in Mishpatim, someone harder to be kind to.

Say there's a neighbor nobody on the street gets along with. Maybe he called the city about a fence. Maybe she said something at a meeting that still stings. People time their trips to the mailbox. Then one morning, out the window, his dog has gotten loose and is trotting toward the highway. Or her car is stuck in the snow, wheels spinning. Nobody else is around. The Torah, in the middle of laws about honest courts, imagines exactly this moment, in a world of oxen and donkeys.
screen: `THE NEIGHBOR NOBODY GETS ALONG WITH.` → `HIS DOG, LOOSE.` → `NOBODY ELSE AROUND.`

segments.voice: The first law, in the old Jewish translation: "If thou meet thine enemy's ox or his ass going astray," you must bring it back to him. Not a friend's. Your enemy's. The second law goes further. You see the donkey of someone who hates you lying under its load, and you may want to walk past. Don't. Help him release it. The Hebrew plays on words: you might want to leave him, azov, but you must help, also azov, a twin verb meaning to unload. And the verse says help with him. Rashi points out: with him. The owner works too; it's a job for both of you, side by side, hands on the same ropes. Notice what the Torah doesn't say. It doesn't say you have to like him, or that the grudge is wrong. It says the animal is suffering and his loss is still a loss, so act anyway. The Talmud pushes the idea one step further. Suppose a friend's donkey needs unloading and an enemy's needs loading. Normally the animal in pain comes first. But here, the Talmud says, help your enemy first, in order to bend your own inclination. The point isn't only the donkey. It's what happens between two people who have pulled on the same rope in the mud.
screen: `RETURN YOUR ENEMY'S OX.` · `AZOV AND AZOV: LEAVE, OR UNLOAD.` · `RASHI: WITH HIM, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE TALMUD: ENEMY FIRST.` · then, large: `HELP YOUR ENEMY'S DONKEY.`

segments.voice: Think of someone ordinary and irritating, not your worst enemy, and picture them stuck: a flat tire, a dropped box of groceries, a crashed laptop the night before a deadline. Picture yourself walking over, not liking them, just helping, your hands and theirs on the same problem. If you pray, you can hold them there for a moment.
Mishpatim. The ordinances. Today, the law that sends you back with your enemy's ox, and to his fallen donkey, to help with him.
Your line: help your enemy's donkey. A week since Sinai: one heart, eagles' wings, the first word and the last, the details, the stranger. That's day three hundred fifty.
